Central Sleep Apnea and Stiff Person Syndrome:
A Case Report
To the Editor :
Stiff person syndrome is a rare neurological condition with
an estimated prevalence of one case per million. Individuals
afﬂicted by this condition typically experience ﬂuctuating
rigidity and muscle spasms affecting axial and limb muscles.
We report a patient with stiff person syndrome and concomitant
central sleep apnea, and we speculate on possible mechanisms
of association.
Case Report
A 60-year-old man complained of excessive daytime sleepiness
(Epworth sleepiness scale, 18/24) and nonrestorative sleep. His
spouse reported breathing pauses but no snoring.
A diagnosis of classic stiff person syndrome had been made
by corroborating his clinical presentation (stiffness in trunk
and in lumbar and abdominal muscles, hyperlordosis) with
electromyographic ﬁndings, which included continuous motor

activity and positive antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD) (2,339 cpm; normal value , 180 cpm). His disease was
treated by intravenous immunoglobulin infusions. Comorbidities
included type 1 diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, Hashimoto thyroiditis,
and hypertension. His body mass index was 29 kg/m
2. There were
no signs of heart failure on physical examination.
Ventilatory polygraphy recorded respiratory events in a
periodic breathing pattern (Figure 1). Summary statistics
demonstrated an apnea –hypopnea index (AHI) of 83/h, a
predominance of central apneas (245 central apneas, 133
obstructive apneas, and 41 mixed apneas), and a mean oxygen
saturation as measured by pulse oximetry (Sp
O2) of 90%; he spent
42% of the sleep time with Sp O2 less than 90%. Lung function
testing was remarkable for a restrictive ventilatory de ﬁcit
(VC = 72% predicted; FEV 1 = 77% predicted; total pulmonary
capacity = 67% predicted). Measurement of blood gas tensions
showed a respiratory alkalosis and mild hypoxemia (pH = 7.48;
PaCO2 = 35 mm Hg; Pa O2 = 77 mm Hg).
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed a normal left
ventricular ejection fraction of 69%. The ventilatory response to
carbon dioxide measured by the rebreathing technique was elevated
(F
IO2 =9 5 % ; FICO2 = 5%; resting _VE = 14.2 L/min; end-tidal [partial]
carbon dioxide pressure [P ETCO2] = 33.5 mm Hg; _VE/PETCO2 =
7.5 L/min/mm Hg) (Figure 2). A brain magnetic resonance imaging
study showed no abnormality, particularly in the brainstem.
Adaptive servo-ventilation (AutoSetCS2; Resmed, St. Priest,
France) was introduced (pressure support, 3 –10 cm H
2O;
expiratory positive airway pressure, 5 cm H 2O) allowing
correction of AHI (to AHI = 4) and hypoxemia (mean Sp O2 = 94%;
time spent with Sp O2 , 90%, 0%). He quickly achieved optimal
adherence to the servo-ventilation device (7.5 h/night), and his
Epworth sleepiness scale scores were signi ﬁcantly improved
(ranging 1 –8 at his follow-up visits).
Discussion
There are three recognized variants of stiff person syndrome (1 –3):
classic stiff person syndrome, stiff leg syndrome, and progressive
encephalomyelitis. The onset of classic stiff person syndrome
is generally insidious, with painful lumbar stiffness, sometimes
associated with muscle spasms that can cause falls. The stiffness
progresses to the proximal and then to the distal limb muscles
and can lead to abnormal postures. Stiff leg syndrome is a focal
variant of stiff person syndrome. Initially, muscle stiffness and
painful spasms are con ﬁned to the distal lower limbs before
reaching the upper limbs and trunk. The third form, progressive
encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus, is characterized
by rapid evolution to severe impairment. Stiff person syndrome
is often associated with one or more autoimmune disorders,
including type 1 diabetes mellitus, Hashimoto thyroiditis, vitiligo,
and myasthenia gravis. Our patient has classic stiff person
syndrome with several associated autoimmune disorders.
The high prevalence of anti-GAD antibodies (60 –80% of
cases) suggests an autoimmune pathogenesis (1, 2). GAD is an

enzyme involved in g-aminobutyric acid (GABA) synthesis. Anti-
GAD antibodies cause inhibition of GABAergic neurons,
responsible for neuronal hyperexcitability. Epilepsy or cerebellar
ataxia may be associated with anti-GAD antibodies (2, 4).
Central sleep apnea is usually brought about by one of two
mechanisms: (1) hypoventilation in patients with impaired central
drive ( “won’t breathe ”) observed in association with congenital
central hypoventilation syndrome, tumors or trauma-induced
lesions to brainstem, obesity hypoventilation syndrome, or use of
an opioid; ( 2) hyperventilation with unstable ventilatory control
and elevated loop gain, which is observed in patients with
congestive heart failure, patients at high altitude, or patients
with idiopathic central sleep apnea. In these conditions,
patients chronically hyperventilate owing to increased
chemoresponsiveness.
Treatment of central sleep apnea varies according to etiology
(5–7). The ﬁrst step is to treat the underlying cause or aggravating
factor(s). In central sleep apnea due to impaired central drive, the
main treatment is noninvasive bi-level positive airway pressure
ventilation (7). In central sleep apnea due to unstable ventilatory
control, continuous positive airway pressure is the primary option.
If this fails, adaptive servo-ventilation is a second option, except in
patients with congestive heart failure with left ventricular ejection
fraction , 45% (8).
In our patient, central sleep apnea was highly periodic, with a
ventilatory length of 10 to 12 seconds and an apnea length of
8 to 10 seconds representing a total cycle length of 20 seconds.
Thus, the duty ratio was 0.6 and the loop gain was approximately
1.4, in favor of ventilatory instability (9). This, combined with high
_VE/PETCO2, led us to conclude that elevated chemosensitivity was
the likely mechanism underlying this patient ’s central sleep apnea.
To our knowledge, this is the second reported case of an
association between stiff person syndrome and central sleep apnea
(10). Two rare conditions may have occurred concomitantly
by chance in both instances, or they might be associated
mechanistically. Several hypotheses can be entertained to link
the two conditions. First, anti-GAD antibodies might cause
brainstem injury. However, hypercapnia would be expected in
this setting, which was not the case in our patient. Second, GABA
inhibition could play a role. CO 2-inhibiting neurons in the
medullary raphe are GABAergics (11). Inhibition of both raphe
and retrotrapezoid neurons with a GABA receptor agonist causes
hypoventilation and reduces the ventilatory response to CO 2 (12).
Thus, the inhibitory effects of anti-GAD antibodies on GABAergic
neurons could increase the activity of the automatic respiratory
centers and the ventilatory response to CO 2. Finally, stiff person
syndrome can cause restrictive chest physiology, which may
explain the relatively low Sp O2 (94%) in our patient that persisted
after central sleep apnea was eliminated with treatment.
Our patient ’s excessive ventilatory response to CO 2 suggests
that his central sleep apnea may be explained by an increased
activity and responsiveness of the brainstem respiratory centers.
We speculate that his brainstem dysfunction may result from
GABA inhibition by circulating anti-GAD antibodies.
